title: The Endemic Baseline: When B_reference Was Never Set
description:
The MBD framework models cognition as deviation from a reference baseline: B(t+1) = B(t)·(1−λ) + I(t)·λ. Every prior paper in the series assumes that Breference encodes a prior legitimate healthy state — an origin from which the system can be understood to have deviated. This paper examines the failure mode that violates that assumption.

The endemic baseline is the condition in which B(0) was itself constructed during chronic disruption. The storm-born agent has never occupied a stable healthy state; their reference vector does not point toward health — it is the pathology. The mathematics of MBD do not change under this condition. The meaning of every quantity in them inverts.

Three specific consequences are derived and computationally demonstrated. (1) Healthy-input rejection: for the storm-born agent, a positive input produces maximum novelty — because the input falls outside Hagent, the set of states ever occupied — and is therefore maximally destabilizing rather than integrative. Under the low-kappa conditions common in chronically disrupted agents, this produces active rejection. The agent's own cognitive architecture enforces the boundary. (2) Horizon invisibility: the Horizon H = Haccessible \ Hagent contains states the agent's neurobiology could reach but has never encoded. For the storm-born agent, the entire healthy region lies in H. Recovery requires navigating to a destination that is, by construction, unrepresentable from the current position. (3) Intervention failure: standard restoration-to-baseline logic fails structurally. When Breference is the pathology, restoration is regression.

The Re-zeroing Protocol is derived from first principles as the corrective framework: a kappa-building phase establishes a high-coupling relationship before any healthy input is introduced; micro-excursions into the Horizon are calibrated just above the novelty threshold; the subsequent destabilization is held as the navigational cost of reaching a previously unreachable attractor, not as evidence of failure.

Two executable computational labs are included. Lab 7a demonstrates the three failure modes by running three agents with identical healthy inputs against different reference structures (neurotypical, acute-onset, and storm-born). Lab 7b runs three intervention strategies — flood, re-zeroing, and premature withdrawal — against identical storm-born agents, demonstrating the predicted outcome hierarchy. The paper and the labs are the same repository; the formal mathematics and the Python simulation are parallel expressions of the same claims.

This paper is a formal dependency of Paper 8 (The Suppressive and Emergent Phenomenon), which extends the Horizon H from a description of circumstantial pathology to a manipulable control surface under adversarial conditions.
